title: Covalent and dative bonding; Lewis structures; Metallic bonding and comparing structures
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BD06#t4 term and clue written for the game; BD02#t3 term and clue written for the game; BD06#t3 term and clue written for the game; BD02#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BD02#N.2, BD06#N.3a, BD02#N.11, BD06#N.11, BD02#N.12b, BD06#N.13, BD06#N.15.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Ductile
items.clue: Able to be drawn into wires, because layers of ions slide.

items.label: Octet rule
items.clue: The tendency of atoms to end up with eight outer electrons.

items.label: Malleable
items.clue: Able to be hammered into shape, because layers of ions slide.

items.label: Lone pair
items.clue: Two outer electrons on an atom that are not shared with another atom.

questions.stem: What holds the hydrogen atom and the chlorine atom together in a molecule of hydrogen chloride, HCl?

options.text: The need of each atom to gain a full outer shell by sharing a pair of electrons
The shared pair of electrons itself, acting as a physical link between the atoms
The electrostatic attraction of both nuclei to a shared pair of electrons
The electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions H⁺ and Cl⁻

questions.explanation: The shared pair lies between the H and Cl nuclei and is attracted to both. That attraction is the covalent bond.

questions.stem: Aluminium is rolled into kitchen foil less than 0.02 mm thick without cracking. Which statement explains this property of aluminium?

options.text: Its layers of cations slide, staying attracted to the delocalised electrons around them.
Its metallic bonds are weak, so the rollers can easily push its atoms apart.
Its bonds between neighbouring atoms bend like hinges instead of breaking.
Its individual atoms are soft, so each one is flattened as it passes between the rollers.

questions.explanation: Metallic bonding is non-directional, so the delocalised electrons keep attracting the cations after the layers have slid. The metal changes shape without cracking.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃, reacts with a hydrogen ion, H⁺, to form the ammonium ion, NH₄⁺. Which statement about the bonds in NH₄⁺ is correct?

options.text: The bond formed from the lone pair on nitrogen is longer and weaker than the other three N–H bonds
The new bond formed from a pair of electrons supplied by the H⁺ ion to nitrogen
The new bond formed from one electron supplied by nitrogen and one electron supplied by H⁺
All four N–H bonds are identical, although one formed from the lone pair on nitrogen

questions.explanation: The new bond is co-ordinate: both electrons from N. Once formed, all four N–H bonds have the same length and strength.

questions.stem: Four solids, P, Q, R and S, are tested. - P: melts at 801 °C; conducts when molten but not as a solid; dissolves in water. - Q: melts at 1085 °C; conducts as a solid and when molten; insoluble in water. - R: melts at 114 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water. - S: melts at 1710 °C; does not conduct as a solid or when molten; insoluble in water. Which pairing of substance and structure is correct?

options.text: P is metallic, because it conducts when molten.
Q is ionic, because it conducts when molten.
R is molecular, because it melts low and never conducts.
S is ionic, because its melting point is very high.

questions.stem: Carbon monoxide, CO, has 10 outer electrons, the same as N₂. Like N₂, it has a triple bond and one lone pair on each atom. Which describes the three shared pairs?

options.text: Three ordinary covalent bonds: C and O each supply three electrons.
Two ordinary covalent bonds, plus one co-ordinate bond from C to O.
Three co-ordinate bonds, all from O to C.
Two ordinary covalent bonds, plus one co-ordinate bond from O to C.

questions.explanation: C shares two electrons and O two: two ordinary pairs. O then donates one lone pair to C: C≡O with an arrow O→C. Each atom keeps one lone pair and has 8.

questions.stem: Silicon melts at 1414 °C. Phosphorus (white, P₄) melts at 44 °C. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: Phosphorus has weaker metallic bonding, because its atoms are larger than silicon atoms.
Silicon is giant covalent, so covalent bonds break; phosphorus is P₄ molecules held by weak London forces.
Melting phosphorus breaks its P–P covalent bonds, which are much weaker than Si–Si bonds.
Silicon atoms have more electrons than P₄ molecules, so London forces between them are stronger.

questions.explanation: Melting silicon breaks strong Si–Si covalent bonds throughout the lattice. Melting P₄ overcomes only weak forces between molecules; the P–P bonds stay intact.

questions.stem: Each liquid is tested with two electrodes and a bulb. Which liquid will not conduct electricity?

options.text: Molten sodium chloride at 850 °C
Liquid mercury at 20 °C
Liquid titanium(IV) chloride, TiCl₄, at 20 °C
Molten aluminium at 700 °C

questions.explanation: TiCl₄ (boils at 136 °C) is made of small covalent molecules. With no ions and no delocalised electrons, nothing carries charge, even though titanium is a metal.
